- [x] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. If you'd like to propose a new feature or change, please open an issue to discuss the change or find an existing issue.

Add AbortLink to cancel browser operations with a CancellationToken

## Description

This implements the design in #70044. It adds the internal `AbortLink`, the factory that creates it, and their tests. The public API does not change, and no family uses `AbortLink` yet. The first one will be Fetch (#69882), and its proposal (#70046) already builds on this design. With this merged first, the Fetch PR can use the real type. The open question in #70044 (a small function in the JS module of the package to save round trips) does not block this PR, because it would change only internals.

### AbortLinkFactory and AbortLink

`FeatureContext.AbortLinkFactory` is an `AbortLinkFactory` shared by the scope. A projection receives it when it is created, as it receives `CreateEventListenerCollection()`. For each operation, the family calls `CreateAsync(cancellationToken)`. It creates a browser `AbortController` with `InvokeConstructorAsync`, reads its `signal` as an object reference, and registers a callback on the token that calls `abort()`. The family passes `Signal` to the browser operation, and calls the operation through `IJSRuntime` with `CancellationToken.None`. The issue explains why.

A few details are worth a look.

- The two setup calls (the constructor and `signal`) use the overloads without a token, so they keep the default interop timeout. Only the browser operation itself runs with `CancellationToken.None`.
- `CreateAsync` returns `null` for a token that cannot be canceled, so a call without a token costs nothing. For a token that is already canceled, or after the scope has ended, it throws before any interop call.
- If the token is canceled or the scope ends while the setup calls run, `CreateAsync` disposes both references and throws, before it registers the callback. If the token is canceled just before `Register`, `Register` runs the callback at once, so the abort is not lost.
- The factory keeps the links that are still open. When the scope ends, `FeatureContext` disposes the factory, and the factory disposes those links, so their callbacks leave the tokens. A token that outlives the circuit can no longer keep the circuit alive through an operation that never ended. A failure there is logged, because scope disposal does not throw.
- The callback runs on the thread that cancels the token. It sends `abort()` and changes no state, so it needs no lock. It ignores `JSDisconnectedException` (the circuit is gone, and the operation with it) and logs any other failure.
- Everything else runs on the scope's synchronization context, as in the event listener code, so there is no `ConfigureAwait(false)` and the list of open links has no lock.
- `DisposeAsync` removes the link from the factory and the callback from the token first. `CancellationTokenRegistration.DisposeAsync` waits for a callback that is running, so no `abort()` goes to a disposed reference. It then disposes the two references, the signal also when releasing the controller fails. `JSObjectReference.DisposeAsync` already ignores `JSDisconnectedException`, so `DisposeAsync` has no `catch`.
- `FeatureContext` keeps the factory in a field typed as `IInternalAsyncDisposal`, as it does for the callback factory of events, so an app that never cancels a browser operation does not keep the type.
- `CreateCanceledException` builds the `OperationCanceledException` that a family throws when its interop call fails after the token was canceled. It keeps the browser error as `InnerException`.

### Tests

- `AbortLinkTest` has 16 unit tests that go through `FeatureContext` with a recording fake. The fake leaves the overloads with a token unimplemented, so a call that passes a token fails the test. The tests cover the token that cannot be canceled, the canceled token, cancellation during setup, a failing setup, disposal (also when releasing the controller fails), the release of open links at the end of the scope (once only, and also when the scope ends during setup), a closed circuit and another failure of `abort()`, and `CreateCanceledException`.
- `AbortLinkTests` has 3 E2E tests in both render modes. A small feature in the test app calls `fetch` the way a family would, and gets itself with `Window.GetOrAddFeature` and `context.AbortLinkFactory`. The test app server holds a request until the browser aborts it, and records what happened. The tests wait for that record through a request that the server answers when the state is reached, so no step depends on a delay. They cover a request that is left alone, an abort before the headers (canceled from a thread pool thread, as a timer does) and while the body is read, and a token that is already canceled, for which no request is sent. The page uses the result marker of the other E2E tests.
- All 105 unit tests of the package pass. All 16 E2E tests of the package pass with `dotnet run` and from the output of `dotnet publish`. When I removed the `abort()` call from `AbortLink`, `AbortLink_AbortsTheRequestInTheBrowserWhenTheTokenIsCanceled` failed, so the test depends on the real abort. The E2E tests run in Chromium only.
- The release at the end of the scope has the same kind of check. Without the loop in `AbortLinkFactory`'s disposal, `ScopeDisposal_ReleasesTheLinksStillOpen` fails. Without the `_disposed` check after the setup calls, `CreateAsync_ThrowsAndReleasesTheReferencesWhenTheScopeEndsDuringCreation` fails.
- In a trimmed WebAssembly app that never uses `context.AbortLinkFactory`, `AbortLink`, `AbortLinkFactory`, and their log messages are removed. Only the `FeatureContext` field stays, as the field for the callback factory of events does.

### What I checked in other browsers

Before this PR, I checked the idea in a scratch app that is not in this PR. It calls `fetch` through plain `IJSRuntime` calls, and its server records whether the browser aborted each request. I ran it in Interactive Server and WebAssembly, in Chromium, Firefox, and the WebKit build that Playwright ships for Windows. The results were the same in all six.

| Scenario | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Token passed to `IJSRuntime` only | .NET throws `TaskCanceledException`, but the server request runs to completion. |
| `abort()` while waiting for the headers | `fetch` rejects at once and the server sees the abort. |
| `abort()` after `fetch` resolved, while `text()` reads the body | `text()` rejects and the server sees the abort. |
| Signal that is already aborted | `fetch` rejects at once and no request reaches the server. |
| `abort()` from `token.Register` in Interactive Server | Works, also when the callback runs outside the circuit's sync context. |
| Error text of an abort | Chromium "signal is aborted without reason" (and "The user aborted a request." while reading the body), Firefox "The operation was aborted.", WebKit "Fetch is aborted". WebKit ignores a reason passed to `abort()`. |

The error text differs by browser, so `AbortLink` never reads it. A family decides by `token.IsCancellationRequested`.

Contributes to #70044

items.title: [Review agent] Calibrate Blazor DI scope teardown IJSObjectReference disposal findings (#69970, #70340)

labels.name: area-infrastructure
labels.description: Includes: MSBuild projects/targets, build scripts, CI, Installers and shared framework

items.body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe the problem.

Across two `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Platform` PRs (#69970 and #70340), review passes produced `P2` lifecycle findings around `IJSObjectReference` disposal during Blazor DI scope teardown (`IInternalAsyncDisposal.InternalDisposeAsync`) without establishing a reachable production trigger or accounting for existing repository conventions:

1. **Non-waiting pending acquisition at DI scope disposal (`#69970` `Screen.cs:103` and `#70340` `Window.cs:88`):**
   - In `Screen.cs` (#69970) and `Window.cs` (#70340), `GetReferenceAsync()` caches `_jsRuntime.GetValueAsync<IJSObjectReference>(...).AsTask()`, and `InternalDisposeAsync()` intentionally only disposes `_referenceTask.Result` when `_referenceTask is { IsCompletedSuccessfully: true }` with the comment:
     ```csharp
     // Don't wait for a pending acquisition. It could hold up scope disposal until the JS interop timeout.
     if (_referenceTask is { IsCompletedSuccessfully: true } referenceTask)
     {
         await referenceTask.Result.DisposeAsync().ConfigureAwait(false);
     }
     ```
   - Review arms (a review model and a review model on #69970; a review model on #70340) flagged a `P2` leak if the scope is disposed while `GetReferenceAsync()` is still in flight and the JS reference arrives afterward.
   - While the source-level mechanism is conditionally possible if an `IJSRuntime` completes `GetValueAsync` after `InternalDisposeAsync` checks `_referenceTask.IsCompletedSuccessfully` (and `JSCallbackFactory.ImportModuleAsync` in #70340 explicitly disposes a late-arriving module to satisfy `BrowserJSRuntime` unit tests that call `ServiceProvider.DisposeAsync()` while holding `"import"`), this exact non-waiting pattern is already established in `Storage.cs:111-115` and `CookieStore.cs:179-183` on `main`.
   - Furthermore, `Window.AddEventListenerAsync` already throws `ObjectDisposedException` after `await GetReferenceAsync()` (`Window.cs:70`), and as the author explained in [#69970 comment `4489650667`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69970#discussion_r4489650667), Blazor DI scope disposal in supported hosts runs during Interactive Server circuit teardown (where inbound interop completion and disposal are serialized on the circuit/renderer dispatcher) or WebAssembly page unload — so a `P2` production leak claim is not established without a concrete supported-host trigger.

2. **Exception propagation during `IJSObjectReference.DisposeAsync` at DI scope disposal (`#70340` `Window.cs:159`, CCR comment [`4489112121`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70340#discussion_r4489112121)):**
   - Separately from the pending-acquisition pattern above, CCR comment `4489112121` (and corroborating review notes) claimed that `await referenceTask.Result.DisposeAsync()` in `Window.InternalDisposeAsync()` could throw `JSDisconnectedException` or `TaskCanceledException` during circuit teardown and skip subsequent feature cleanup.
   - As the author noted in [#70340 comment `4489969683`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70340#discussion_r4489969683), `CircuitHost.DisposeAsync` calls `JSRuntime.MarkPermanentlyDisconnected()` before disposing the DI scope (preventing new outbound calls from being sent), and `JSObjectReference.DisposeAsync` already suppresses `JSDisconnectedException` (since #64773).

### Describe the solution you'd like

1. **Calibrate Blazor Components / JSInterop review guidance (`docs/BlazorComponentsGuidance.md` and/or `.github/agents/review-candidate-verifier.agent.md`):**
   - Document the Blazor DI scope teardown contract for scoped JS interop projections (`Window`, `Screen`, `Storage`, `CookieStore`):
     - In Interactive Server, `CircuitHost` marks `JSRuntime` permanently disconnected before scope disposal runs, inbound completions are coordinated through the circuit/renderer dispatcher, and `JSObjectReference.DisposeAsync` already ignores `JSDisconnectedException`.
     - In WebAssembly, the DI scope for browser platform services lives until page unload.
     - Non-waiting disposal of a lazy `Task<IJSObjectReference>` (`if (_referenceTask is { IsCompletedSuccessfully: true })`) that matches existing `Storage`/`CookieStore` conventions is intentional so scope disposal cannot hang on a pending JS interop call, and should not be elevated as a `P2` blocking production leak unless a reachable non-teardown disposal path is established in the PR.
2. **Require `review-candidate-verifier` to check existing sibling conventions and `JSObjectReference.DisposeAsync` exception contracts:**
   - Before keeping a `P2` disposal-leak or `JSDisconnectedException` propagation candidate on an `IJSObjectReference`, verify whether `JSObjectReference.DisposeAsync` already suppresses the claimed exception and whether the disposal path is reachable in a supported host outside circuit/page teardown.

### Additional context

- Tracked under #70231.
- Evidence PRs:
  - #69970 (`src/Components/Platform/src/Screen.cs:103`, author explanation in [`4489650667`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69970#discussion_r4489650667))
  - #70340 (`src/Components/Platform/src/Window.cs:88` and `Window.cs:159`, author explanation in [`4489969683`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/70340#discussion_r4489969683))

items.title: Add InvokeNew, GetValue & SetValue to JS interop API
items.body:
## Description

Adds three new methods to the JS interop API and refactors existing interop communication to pass arguments using a `JsInvocationInfo` object.

The API design is based on conclusions in https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/31151#issuecomment-2703660318.

## Changes

- Adds the following async methods:
	- `ValueTask<IJSObjectReference> InvokeNewAsync(string identifier, object?[]? args)`
	- `ValueTask<TValue> GetValueAsync<TValue>(string identifier)`
	- `ValueTask SetValueAsync<TValue>(string identifier, TValue value)`
	- The methods are added to `IJSRuntime` and `IJSObjectReference` and their implementations with the same scoping behavior as the existing `InvokeAsync` method.
	- Overloads that take a `CancellationToken` argument, `TimeSpan` timeout argument, or `params object?[]? args` argument are also added to be consistent with the overloads of `InvokeAsync`.
	- There is a special overload `IJSObjectReference.GetValueAsync<TValue>()` that does not take and identifier and simply returns the value of the object (`TValue` is here meant to be a model of the object's properties that the caller is interested in).
- Adds the following synchronous methods:
	- `IJSInProcessObjectReference InvokeNew(string identifier, params object?[]? args)`
	- `TValue GetValue<TValue>(string identifier)`
	- `void SetValue<TValue>(string identifier, TValue value)`
	- The methods are added to `IJSInProcessRuntime` and `IJSInProcessObjectReference` and their implementations with the same scoping behavior as the existing `Invoke` method.
- ~~Refactors the existing interop bridge methods (e.g. `BeginInvokeJS` and `InvokeJS` on the .NET side) that previously passed interop call configuration as separate arguments. The configuration is now packaged into a `JSInvocationInfo` object which is serialized as JSON string (using a source generated JsonSerializer). Motivation for this change was to make the interop communication across the various supported channels better maintainable and extensible going forward.~~
- Extends the `Microsoft.JSInterop.JS` library to support the new interop methods, including reading and modifying object properties and invoking constructor functions with the `new` keyword.
- Adds Jest tests for the new functionality in the `Microsoft.JSInterop.JS` library.
- Adds cases for the new functionality to the existing `InteropTest` in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.E2ETests`.
- Adds `DotNetToJSInterop.razor` component to `BasicTestApp` intended for manual testing and debugging of the JS interop functionality on different platforms.

For other types of questions, consider using [StackOverflow](https://stackoverflow.com).

-->

### Describe the bug
After KB5003637 was installed by Windows Update last night, my Blazor application which runs on .Net 5 & .Net 6 Preview 4 began to exhibit failures in the GRPC stack. 

### To Reproduce
Run a Blazor GRPC client & server on a system updated to that Windows cumulative patch. Run multiple GRPC client requests for data. Randomly, the GRPC server service will fail with an exception of "GRPC client service can't connect because the target machine actively refused it"

As an aside I also saw multiple Blazor component instantiation failures that related to JSON deserialization. I did not capture those exceptions in detail. I presume that they are somehow related to SignalR disruptions

Removing the update restored proper functionality to both versions of my application.

items.title: Wrong nullable annotations for JSRuntimeExtensions.InvokeVoidAsync

labels.name: bug
labels.description: This issue describes a behavior which is not expected - a bug.

items.body:
## Summary

 The nullable annotations of `JSRuntimeExtensions.InvokeVoidAsync` seems not good for the params parameter. I think it should match the annotations of `JSRuntimeExtensions.InvokeAsync`

Current method signature

````csharp
public static async ValueTask InvokeVoidAsync(this IJSRuntime jsRuntime, string identifier, params object[] args)
// Same for other overloads
````

Expected signature

````c#
public static async ValueTask InvokeVoidAsync(this IJSRuntime jsRuntime, string identifier, params object?[]? args)
````

## Additional notes

The nullable annotations are inconsistent for `params` parameters in this project

1. List of methods with `params object[]` (seems not good)

	static Microsoft.JSInterop.JSRuntimeExtensions.InvokeVoidAsync(this Microsoft.JSInterop.IJSRuntime! jsRuntime, string! identifier, System.Threading.CancellationToken cancellationToken, params object![]! args) -> System.Threading.Tasks.ValueTask

	static Microsoft.JSInterop.JSObjectReferenceExtensions.InvokeAsync<TValue>(this Microsoft.JSInterop.IJSObjectReference! jsObjectReference, string! identifier, params object?[]! args) -> System.Threading.Tasks.ValueTask<TValue>
	static Microsoft.JSInterop.JSObjectReferenceExtensions.InvokeVoidAsync(this Microsoft.JSInterop.IJSObjectReference! jsObjectReference, string! identifier, System.Threading.CancellationToken cancellationToken, params object?[]! args) -> System.Threading.Tasks.ValueTask
	static Microsoft.JSInterop.JSObjectReferenceExtensions.InvokeVoidAsync(this Microsoft.JSInterop.IJSObjectReference! jsObjectReference, string! identifier, System.TimeSpan timeout, params object?[]! args) -> System.Threading.Tasks.ValueTask
	static Microsoft.JSInterop.JSObjectReferenceExtensions.InvokeVoidAsync(this Microsoft.JSInterop.IJSObjectReference! jsObjectReference, string! identifier, params object?[]! args) -> System.Threading.Tasks.ValueTask

    ````

3. List of methods with `params object?[]?`

    ````
	Microsoft.JSInterop.IJSInProcessObjectReference.Invoke<TValue>(string! identifier, params object?[]? args) -> TValue
	Microsoft.JSInterop.IJSInProcessRuntime.Invoke<TResult>(string! identifier, params object?[]? args) -> TResult
	Microsoft.JSInterop.Implementation.JSInProcessObjectReference.Invoke<TValue>(string! identifier, params object?[]? args) -> TValue
	Microsoft.JSInterop.JSInProcessRuntime.Invoke<TValue>(string! identifier, params object?[]? args) -> TValue
	static Microsoft.JSInterop.JSRuntimeExtensions.InvokeAsync<TValue>(this Microsoft.JSInterop.IJSRuntime! jsRuntime, string! identifier, System.Threading.CancellationToken cancellationToken, params object?[]? args) -> System.Threading.Tasks.ValueTask<TValue>

	static Microsoft.JSInterop.JSRuntimeExtensions.InvokeAsync<TValue>(this Microsoft.JSInterop.IJSRuntime! jsRuntime, string! identifier, params object?[]? args) -> System.Threading.Tasks.ValueTask<TValue>

Should they all be updated to `params object?[]?`?

### Summary
- Migrated `InputFile` from https://github.com/SteveSandersonMS/BlazorInputFile to `M.A.C.Web.Extensions`
- Removed dependency on third-party base64 encoding JS code.
- Added `IJSUnmarshalledRuntime` to allow `RemoteFileListEntryStream` to make unmarshalled JS invocations without reflection.
- Reimplemented `RemoteFileListEntryStream` to use `System.IO.Pipelines`.
- Added E2E tests

Addresses #12205

items.title: JSObjectReference
items.body:
### Summary
* Modified JS interop to use the new [`mono_wasm_invoke_js_blazor`](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/f309b53d4e435dbe4a7945676d167ef910959403/src/mono/wasm/runtime/dotnet_support.js#L33) function.
* Added support for indicating special JS interop return values (e.g., a `JSObjectReference`), along with the ability to specify which object instance is handling the invocation.
* Added `JSObjectReference`, which supports invoking functions from JS objects.
* Added the ability to pass a `JSObjectReference` instance as a parameter to a JS interop call.
* Added support for synchronous JS interop calls via `JSInProcessObjectReference`.
* Added `DotNet.createJSObjectReference` to allow passing JS objects to .NET. and `DotNet.disposeJSObjectReference` to allow disposal from JS when it's most convenient.
* Added some functional/E2E tests.

### TODO
* ~~Add support for unmarshalled JS interop calls via `JSUnmarshalledObjectReference` (dependent on #24640).~~
  * Update: This will likely get done in a follow-up PR, as it's not a critical piece of functionality.

Addresses #24648
